notes.title: Lahore Resolution 1940 — Constitutional & Historical Analysis
notes.summary: Passed on 23 March 1940 at Minto Park (now Iqbal Park), Lahore. Presented by A.K. Fazlul Haq demanding independent states for Muslims in the north-western and eastern zones of British India.

pages.heading: Lahore Resolution 1940 — Constitutional & Historical Analysis
pages.subheading: Pakistan Studies • EXAMORA PAKISTAN Study Note
paragraphs: The Lahore Resolution (Qarardad-e-Lahore), later popularly known as the Pakistan Resolution, was formally adopted during the three-day 27th Annual Session of the All-India Muslim League held at Minto Park (now Greater Iqbal Park), Lahore, from 22 to 24 March 1940.

Following the resignation of Congress Provincial Ministries in 1939 and the outbreak of World War II, Quaid-e-Azam Muhammad Ali Jinnah presided over the historic gathering of over 100,000 delegates from across British India.

Sher-e-Bangla A.K. Fazlul Haq, the Premier of Bengal, moved the formal resolution on 23 March 1940, which was seconded by Chaudhry Khaliquzzaman, Maulana Zafar Ali Khan, Sardar Aurangzeb Khan, and Sir Abdullah Haroon.
keyPoints: Session Dates: 22–24 March 1940 at Minto Park (Iqbal Park), Lahore.
Presided Over By: Quaid-e-Azam Muhammad Ali Jinnah.
Moved By: A.K. Fazlul Haq (Premier of United Bengal) on 23 March 1940.
Commemorative Monument: Minar-e-Pakistan stands at the exact site.

pages.heading: Core Constitutional Principles of the 1940 Resolution
pages.subheading: Territorial Readjustment & Autonomous Sovereign Units
paragraphs: The resolution declared that no constitutional plan would be workable in the country or acceptable to the Muslims unless geographical contiguous units are demarcated into regions which should be so constituted, with such territorial readjustments as may be necessary.

Specifically, it stipulated that the areas in which the Muslims are numerically in a majority, as in the North-Western and Eastern Zones of India, should be grouped to constitute Independent States in which the constituent units shall be autonomous and sovereign.

Furthermore, the resolution mandated that adequate, effective, and mandatory safeguards shall be specifically provided in the constitution for minorities in these units and in the regions for the protection of their religious, cultural, economic, political, and administrative rights.
keyPoints: Rejected the federal scheme of the Government of India Act 1935.
Demanded demarcation of geographically contiguous Muslim-majority zones.
Guaranteed constitutional safeguards for religious and cultural minorities.

pages.heading: Quaid-e-Azam’s Presidential Address & Two-Nation Theory
pages.subheading: Ideological Foundation of the Pakistan Movement
paragraphs: In his landmark presidential address on 22 March 1940, Quaid-e-Azam articulated the Two-Nation Theory with unmatched constitutional clarity. He emphasized that Hindus and Muslims belong to two different religious philosophies, social customs, and literary traditions.

He explained that Muslim India could not accept any constitution which must necessarily result in a Hindu-majority government across the entire subcontinent, transforming Muslims into a permanent constitutional minority.
This shift marked the transition of the Muslim League from seeking federal safeguards within a united India to demanding sovereign statehood.
keyPoints: Defined Muslims as a ”nation by any definition of the word“ rather than a minority.
Transformed the political trajectory of South Asia within seven years (1940–1947).

pages.heading: 1946 Delhi Legislators Convention & Past Exam MCQs
pages.subheading: High-Yield FPSC / PPSC / CSS Revision Facts
paragraphs: In April 1946, at the All-India Muslim League Legislators Convention in Delhi, Hussain Shaheed Suhrawardy moved a resolution clarifying that the North-Western and Eastern zones would form a single sovereign state of Pakistan.
Within seven years and five months of the Lahore Resolution, Pakistan emerged as an independent sovereign state on 14 August 1947.
keyPoints: Who translated the Lahore Resolution into Urdu? Maulana Zafar Ali Khan.
Who seconded the resolution from Sindh? Sir Abdullah Haroon.
Who seconded the resolution from Balochistan? Qazi Muhammad Isa.
Foundation stone of Minar-e-Pakistan laid: 23 March 1960; completed: October 1968.

notes.title: Human Blood Groups, ABO System & Rh Factor
notes.summary: Complete Everyday Science notes covering antigens, antibodies, universal donor (O−), universal recipient (AB+), and Rh incompatibility.

pages.heading: Discovery of the ABO Blood Group System
pages.subheading: Everyday Science • CSS / PMS / PPSC General Ability
paragraphs: Human blood groups were discovered by Austrian immunologist Karl Landsteiner in 1901, for which he was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1930.

Blood classification is determined by the presence or absence of specific inherited antigenic substances on the surface of Red Blood Cells (erythrocytes) and corresponding antibodies in the blood plasma.
The four primary ABO blood groups are Group A, Group B, Group AB, and Group O.
keyPoints: Discoverer of ABO System: Karl Landsteiner (1901).
Antigens (Agglutinogens): Located on the surface membrane of Red Blood Cells.
Antibodies (Agglutinins): Circulate in the blood plasma.

pages.heading: Antigen-Antibody Matrix & Transfusion Compatibility
pages.subheading: Universal Donor vs. Universal Recipient
paragraphs: Group A possesses A-antigens on red blood cells and anti-B antibodies in the plasma. Group B possesses B-antigens on red blood cells and anti-A antibodies in the plasma.
Group AB possesses both A and B antigens on red blood cells and neither anti-A nor anti-B antibodies in plasma, making AB+ the Universal Plasma Donor and Universal Red Cell Recipient.

Group O possesses neither A nor B antigens on the cell membrane, which prevents agglutination when transfused into patients of other blood types. Specifically, O-negative (O−) is the Universal Red Blood Cell Donor.
keyPoints: Universal Red Cell Donor: O Negative (O−) — lacks A, B, and Rh(D) antigens.
Universal Red Cell Recipient: AB Positive (AB+) — lacks anti-A, anti-B, and anti-Rh antibodies.
Average adult human blood volume: 4.5 to 5.5 liters (approx. 7% of body weight).

pages.heading: Rhesus (Rh) Factor & Erythroblastosis Fetalis
pages.subheading: Clinical Significance & Competitive Exam Takeaways
paragraphs: The Rh factor (Rhesus factor) was discovered by Karl Landsteiner and Alexander S. Wiener in 1940 through experiments with Rhesus monkeys. Individuals who have the D-antigen on their RBCs are Rh-positive (Rh+), while those lacking it are Rh-negative (Rh−).

Rh incompatibility (Erythroblastosis fetalis) can occur when an Rh-negative mother carries an Rh-positive fetus, prompting maternal anti-Rh IgG antibodies to cross the placenta in subsequent pregnancies unless prevented by Rho(D) immune globulin.
keyPoints: Normal pH of human arterial blood: 7.35 to 7.45 (slightly alkaline).
Lifespan of human Red Blood Cells (Erythrocytes): 120 days.
Graveyard of Red Blood Cells: Spleen.

notes.title: 1973 Constitution of Pakistan — Fundamental Rights & Key Articles
notes.summary: Article-by-article breakdown of Part II Chapter 1 (Fundamental Rights), Principles of Policy, and major constitutional amendments.

pages.heading: Promulgation & Salient Features of the 1973 Constitution
pages.subheading: Adopted 10 April 1973 • Enforced 14 August 1973
paragraphs: The Constitution of the Islamic Republic of Pakistan (1973) was unanimously passed by the National Assembly on 10 April 1973 and came into force on 14 August 1973.
It established a parliamentary form of government with a bicameral legislature (Majlis-e-Shoora) comprising the National Assembly (Lower House) and the Senate (Upper House).
keyPoints: Total Articles: 280 Articles divided into 12 Parts and 5 Schedules.
Article 2: Islam shall be the State religion of Pakistan.
Article 2A: Objectives Resolution made a substantive part of the Constitution.

pages.heading: Fundamental Rights (Articles 8 to 28)
pages.subheading: High-Frequency Articles Tested in FPSC, PPSC & CSS
paragraphs: Article 8 declares that any law or custom inconsistent with Fundamental Rights shall be void. Article 9 guarantees Security of Person, while Article 10 provides safeguards as to arrest and detention.
Article 10A (inserted by the 18th Amendment) guarantees the Right to Fair Trial. Article 19 ensures Freedom of Speech, and Article 19A guarantees the Right to Information.
Article 25 guarantees Equality of Citizens before the law, and Article 25A mandates the State to provide free and compulsory education to all children aged 5 to 16 years.
keyPoints: Article 6: High Treason for abrogating or subverting the Constitution.
Article 10A: Right to Fair Trial and due process.
Article 25A: Right to Free & Compulsory Education (ages 5–16).

pages.heading: Landmark Constitutional Amendments Overview
pages.subheading: 18th Amendment (2010) & Provincial Autonomy
paragraphs: The 18th Constitutional Amendment (2010) restored the parliamentary character of the 1973 Constitution, abolished the Concurrent Legislative List, devolved ministries to the provinces, and renamed NWFP as Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.
It also strengthened the Council of Common Interests (CCI) and reformed the judicial appointment procedure through Article 175A.
keyPoints: 1st Amendment (1974): Redefined boundaries of Pakistan.
8th Amendment (1985): Introduced Article 58(2)(b) presidential dissolution power.
18th Amendment (2010): Restored parliamentary supremacy and provincial autonomy.

pdfs.title: Pakistan Affairs — Complete Notes & Chronology (CSS / PMS)

pages.heading: Chapter 1: Reform Movements in South Asian Islam (1700–1900)
pages.subheading: Shah Waliullah, Faraizi Movement & Aligarh Movement
paragraphs: Shah Waliullah (1703–1762) initiated intellectual and socio-political revival among Indian Muslims after the passing of Emperor Aurangzeb. He translated the Holy Quran into Persian (Fath-ur-Rahman) and authored Hujjatullah-il-Baligha.
Haji Shariatullah founded the Faraizi Movement in Eastern Bengal (1818) to protect Muslim peasantry from agrarian exploitation and revive obligatory religious duties.
Sir Syed Ahmad Khan (1817–1898) launched the Aligarh Movement after the War of Independence 1857, founding the Scientific Society (1864) and Muhammadan Anglo-Oriental College at Aligarh (1875).
keyPoints: Shah Waliullah born: 21 February 1703 (Delhi); real name: Qutb-ud-Din Ahmad.
Asbab-e-Baghawat-e-Hind authored by Sir Syed Ahmad Khan in 1859.
MAO College Aligarh elevated to Muslim University in 1920.

pages.heading: Chapter 2: Constitutional Milestones (1905–1935)
pages.subheading: Partition of Bengal, Simla Deputation, Lucknow Pact & Fourteen Points
paragraphs: The Partition of Bengal took place on 16 October 1905 during the viceroyalty of Lord Curzon, creating Eastern Bengal and Assam with Dhaka as capital, before its annulment on 12 December 1911.

On 1 October 1906, a 35-member Muslim delegation led by Sir Sultan Muhammad Shah (Aga Khan III) met Viceroy Lord Minto at Simla to demand separate electorates, which were granted in the Minto-Morley Reforms of 1909.
The All-India Muslim League was founded at Dhaka on 30 December 1906 during the Muhammadan Educational Conference hosted by Nawab Salimullah Khan.
keyPoints: Lucknow Pact (1916): Earned Quaid-e-Azam the title Ambassador of Hindu-Muslim Unity.
Delhi Muslim Proposals: Presented in March 1927.
Quaid-e-Azam’s Fourteen Points: Presented on 28 March 1929 in response to the Nehru Report.

pages.heading: Chapter 3: Allama Iqbal’s Allahabad Address & Round Table Conferences
pages.subheading: 1930–1937 Constitutional Evolution
paragraphs: Delivering the presidential address at the 21st Annual Session of the All-India Muslim League at Allahabad on 29 December 1930, Allama Muhammad Iqbal proposed the amalgamation of Punjab, NWFP, Sindh, and Balochistan into a consolidated North-West Indian Muslim State.

Three Round Table Conferences were held in London between 1930 and 1932, culminating in the Government of India Act 1935, which separated Sindh from Bombay Presidency and introduced provincial autonomy.
keyPoints: Choudhry Rahmat Ali coined the name PAKISTAN in the pamphlet "Now or Never" (28 January 1933).
1937 Provincial Elections and Congress Rule (1937–1939); Day of Deliverance observed on 22 December 1939.

pages.heading: Chapter 4: Post-1947 Early Administrative & Constitutional Challenges
pages.subheading: Objectives Resolution 1949 to the 1956 & 1962 Constitutions
paragraphs: Upon independence on 14 August 1947, Quaid-e-Azam Muhammad Ali Jinnah took oath as the first Governor-General of Pakistan and Nawabzada Liaquat Ali Khan as the first Prime Minister.

On 12 March 1949, the First Constituent Assembly adopted the Objectives Resolution moved by Prime Minister Liaquat Ali Khan, establishing sovereignty of Allah Almighty and democratic principles of social justice.
keyPoints: Pakistan admitted to the United Nations: 30 September 1947.
State Bank of Pakistan inaugurated by Quaid-e-Azam: 1 July 1948.
First Constitution of Pakistan enforced: 23 March 1956.

pdfs.title: Everyday Science & General Ability Handbook (1000+ Key Facts)

pages.heading: Section 1: Physical Sciences, SI Units & Scientific Instruments
pages.subheading: FPSC / PPSC / CSS General Science & Ability
paragraphs: The International System of Units (SI) defines seven base units: meter (length), kilogram (mass), second (time), ampere (electric current), kelvin (thermodynamic temperature), mole (amount of substance), and candela (luminous intensity).

Scientific instruments frequently tested in competitive exams include the Barometer (atmospheric pressure, invented by Evangelista Torricelli), Hygrometer (relative humidity), Anemometer (wind speed), Lactometer (milk purity/density), and Seismograph (earthquake intensity).
keyPoints: Speed of light in vacuum: 2.998 × 10^8 m/s (approx. 300,000 km/s).
Light-year measures astronomical distance (approx. 9.46 × 10^12 km).
1 Astronomical Unit (AU): Mean Earth-Sun distance (~149.6 million km).

pages.heading: Section 2: Vitamins, Deficiencies & Human Physiology
pages.subheading: Fat-Soluble (A, D, E, K) vs. Water-Soluble (B-Complex, C)
paragraphs: Vitamins are organic micronutrients essential for metabolic regulation. Fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K) are stored in adipose tissue and the liver, whereas water-soluble vitamins (Vitamin B-complex and Vitamin C) must be replenished regularly in the diet.

Deficiency of Vitamin A (Retinol) causes Night Blindness (Nyctalopia) and Xerophthalmia. Deficiency of Vitamin B1 (Thiamine) causes Beriberi. Deficiency of Vitamin C (Ascorbic Acid) causes Scurvy. Deficiency of Vitamin D (Calciferol) causes Rickets in children and Osteomalacia in adults.
keyPoints: Vitamin K (Phylloquinone) is essential for blood coagulation (prothrombin synthesis).
Largest gland in the human body: Liver; Largest organ: Skin.
Master endocrine gland: Pituitary gland (located at the base of the brain).

pages.heading: Section 3: Atmospheric Layers & Environmental Science
pages.subheading: Troposphere, Stratosphere, Mesosphere, Thermosphere & Exosphere
paragraphs: Earth’s atmosphere consists of 78.08% Nitrogen, 20.95% Oxygen, 0.93% Argon, and ~0.04% Carbon Dioxide along with trace gases and water vapor.

All weather phenomena occur in the Troposphere (0–12 km). The Stratosphere (12–50 km) contains the Ozone Layer (O3), which absorbs harmful solar ultraviolet (UV-B) radiation. The Mesosphere (50–85 km) is the coldest atmospheric layer where meteors burn up.
keyPoints: Montreal Protocol (1987): Global treaty to phase out ozone-depleting substances (CFCs).
Kyoto Protocol (1997) & Paris Agreement (2015): Greenhouse gas emission frameworks.

pdfs.title: English Precis, Idioms & Pair of Words Compendium

pages.heading: Part 1: Golden Rules of English Precis Writing
pages.subheading: One-Third Length Rule, Third-Person Voice & Objective Tone
paragraphs: A precis is a clear, compact, and logical summary of a passage preserving its essential ideas in roughly one-third of the original word count.

Always write in your own words, use indirect speech and the third-person pronoun, avoid personal commentary or examples not central to the thesis, and assign a concise title reflecting the central theme.
keyPoints: Target Word Count: Strictly 33% (±5 words) of the original passage.
Avoid direct quotations, rhetorical questions, and first-person pronouns.

pages.heading: Part 2: High-Frequency CSS / FPSC Pair of Words
pages.subheading: Distinguishing Homophones & Confusable Lexical Pairs
paragraphs: 1. Affect (verb: to influence) vs. Effect (noun: result; verb: to bring about). 2. Allusion (indirect reference) vs. Illusion (deceptive appearance). 3. Apprise (to inform) vs. Appraise (to assess value).

4. Compliment (expression of praise) vs. Complement (that which completes). 5. Eminent (distinguished/famous) vs. Imminent (about to happen). 6. Judicial (relating to courts) vs. Judicious (wise and prudent).
keyPoints: Discrete (separate/distinct) vs. Discreet (careful/tactful).
Stationary (not moving) vs. Stationery (writing materials).

pages.heading: Part 3: Essential Idiomatic Expressions for Competitive Exams
pages.subheading: Meanings & Contextual Usage
paragraphs:
• A Pyrrhic victory: A victory won at such a devastating cost that it amounts to defeat.
• To cross the Rubicon: To take an irrevocable step.
• To bury the hatchet: To end a quarrel and make peace.
• A white elephant: A costly possession that is burdensome to maintain.
keyPoints: To read between the lines: To discern a hidden or implicit meaning.
Swan song: The final performance or farewell achievement of a career.

pdfs.title: Islamic Studies (Islamiat) — Governance, Human Rights & Seerah

pages.heading: Charter of Madinah (Mithaq-e-Madinah) & Pluralistic Statecraft
pages.subheading: First Written Constitution in World History (1 AH / 622 CE)
paragraphs: Following the Hijrah to Madinah in 622 CE, Prophet Muhammad (PBUH) promulgated the Charter of Madinah (Mithaq-e-Madinah), establishing a multi-religious commonwealth uniting the Muhajirun, Ansar, and Jewish tribes under common citizenship, mutual defense, and freedom of religion.
keyPoints: Total Clauses of Mithaq-e-Madinah: 47 (or 52 in detailed breakdowns).
Treaty of Hudaybiyyah: Concluded in 6 AH (628 CE), termed "Fath-e-Mubeen" (Clear Victory).

pages.heading: The Last Sermon (Khutbah Hajjat-ul-Wida) — Universal Human Rights
pages.subheading: Delivered on 9th Dhul-Hijjah 10 AH (632 CE) at Plain of Arafat
paragraphs: The Farewell Sermon abolished racial superiority, blood feuds of the Pre-Islamic era, and usury (Riba), while establishing the sanctity of life, property, and honor, and guaranteeing the rights of women and laborers.
keyPoints: Abolished Arab vs. non-Arab and white vs. black superiority; Taqwa is the sole criterion of honor.
